question: What command does the LORD give Hosea, and what names do Gomer's three children receive?
The name יִזְרְעֵאל (Yizre’el, “Jezreel,” “God sows”) appears as a threat in verse 4 and as a promise in verse 11: how can the same name carry such different meanings?
How do verses 10 and 11 reverse the names given to the children, and how do Paul and Peter take up this reversal in the New Testament?
God asks the prophet to live out in his own house the message he will proclaim: what part of your life speaks louder than your words?
Who did the woman think gave her bread, wool, linen and oil, and what does the LORD say He will take back?
The name בַּעַל (Ba‘al) was also an ordinary word for “lord” or “husband”: why does verse 16 say the people will no longer call the LORD “my Baal”?
Why does the LORD lead the woman “into the wilderness” to speak “tenderly to her,” and what does it mean that the Valley of Achor becomes “a door of hope”?
The LORD promises to betroth the people “in righteousness and justice, in loving devotion and compassion”: which of these words do you most need to hear today in your relationship with God?
What does Hosea do with the woman in this chapter, how much does he pay, and what condition does he set for the days ahead?
The verb אָהַב (’ahav, “love”) is repeated four times in verse 1, for the prophet, for the LORD and for the people: what does this repetition show about loves in conflict?
What period do verses 4 and 5 describe for Israel, and what does it mean to return to seek “the LORD their God and David their king”?
God loves a people who love other things: how does this persistent love challenge the way you love those who do not love you back?
Of what does the LORD accuse the inhabitants of the land, and what effect does the people's sin have on the land itself and the animals?
The noun דַּעַת (da‘at, “knowledge”) appears in “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge”: what kind of knowledge does the text speak of, and who was responsible for teaching it?
Why does God say He will not punish the daughters and daughters-in-law, and what responsibility does the text place on the men of the people?
What habits help you truly know God, and not merely know things about Him?
To what groups in Israel does the chapter speak, and what images of hunting are used to accuse them?
Why does Ephraim turn to Assyria when it sees its wound, and what does the text say about the result of this search?
The verb בָּקַשׁ (baqash, “seek”) appears when the people go with flocks and herds without finding the LORD, and again in verse 15: what distinguishes one seeking from the other?
The LORD waits for the people to admit their guilt and seek His face: what keeps you from admitting guilt before God?
What do the people say in the invitation “Come, let us return to the LORD,” and what images from nature do they use to speak of God's coming?
How does God's answer in verses 4 to 6 assess the repentance described at the beginning of the chapter?
The word חֵסֵד (chesed, “loving devotion, loyalty”) is compared to the morning mist and then used in “I desire mercy, not sacrifice”: why does Jesus quote this verse in the Gospels?
The people's loyalty was “like the early dew that vanishes”: which of your resolutions usually last a short time, and what would help you keep them?
What image of the oven and the baker does the prophet use to describe the king's court and the conspiracies?
The word תַּנּוּר (tannur, “oven”) returns three times: what does this image of heat held in and then uncontrollable say about the passions described?
What do the comparisons of Ephraim with “an unturned cake” and with “a silly dove” mean?
Ephraim grows old “but he does not notice”: what slow losses in your spiritual life may be going unnoticed?
What accusations does the LORD make against Israel about the kings, the princes and the calf of Samaria?
The verb זָנַח (zanach, “reject”) appears when Israel rejects what is good and when the calf is rejected: how are the two rejections related?
What does the proverb “they sow the wind and reap the whirlwind” say about the relationship between the people's acts and their consequences?
Israel “has forgotten his Maker and built palaces”: how is it possible to build religious things and at the same time forget God?
How do the people treat the prophet in verses 7 and 8, and what comparison is made with the days of Gibeah?
The text calls the נָבִיא (navi’, “prophet”) a fool and a watchman over Ephraim: what do these two descriptions say about the prophet's place among the people?
How does the image of “grapes in the wilderness” and the first fruit on the fig tree show what Israel was for God, and what changed at Baal-peor?
The text asks “what will you do on the appointed day?” of a people who would lose their feasts: what do the celebrations of your faith mean to you when everything is going well?
How does the chapter relate Israel's prosperity to the multiplication of altars and pillars, and what will happen to the calf of Beth-aven?
The word פְּרִי (peri, “fruit”) opens and closes the chapter, from the fruitful vine to the “fruit of lies”: what path does the chapter describe between these two fruits?
What contrast is there between the sowing asked for in verse 12 and the plowing described in verse 13?
“Break up your unplowed ground, for it is time to seek the LORD”: what hardened ground in your life needs to be turned over?
With what gestures of a father does the LORD describe the care He had for Israel since Egypt?
What does the phrase “I am God and not man, the Holy One among you” explain about the decision not to destroy Ephraim?
Verse 9 uses אֵל (’el, “God”) in contrast with “man”: how does this contrast change the way we understand God's anger and compassion in this chapter?
God says He led the people “with cords of love”: in what way do you perceive this care in your story, even when you did not recognize it at the time?
What episodes of Jacob's life does the prophet recall, and in what order?
The verb שׁוּב (shuv) appears in “He will repay him” and in “return to your God”: why does the same verb serve for punishment and for the invitation to return?
What contradiction does the text show between the merchant's dishonest scales and Ephraim's words in verse 8?
“Maintain love and justice, and always wait for your God”: which of these three attitudes is hardest for you now?
How did Ephraim go from exalted to guilty, and with what fleeting images does verse 3 describe his end?
What link does the text make between abundance and forgetting God, and why do the images of God become so threatening?
Verse 14 speaks to שְׁאוֹל (she’ol) and to death with questions: how should we understand these questions here, and how does Paul use them in 1 Corinthians 15?
“When they were satisfied, their hearts became proud”: what care do you take not to forget God when life is going well?
What words does the prophet suggest the people bring to the LORD, and what supports do the people promise to give up?

The verb שׁוּב (shuv) appears in the invitation to the people, in God's anger that turns away and in those who will again dwell in His shade: how does the last chapter tie these movements of return together?
What images of plants and trees does the LORD use for Israel's restoration, and what is said of God in verse 8?
The book ends saying that the ways of the LORD are right and that on the same ways some walk and others stumble: what does this say about the way you walk this path?
